why.correct: The student chose four widths (the factor she changed) and measured the height of the wet front (the response).
options: Correct: she set the width and measured the height.
This reverses them; the height is what she measured, not what she set.
Paper type and time were kept the same for every strip; they are controlled variables.
The time was fixed for all strips, and the width was chosen, not measured.

why.correct: Controlled variables are kept the same for every strip: the same filter paper, the same 10 minutes and the same 1 cm dipped in.
options: Controlled: every strip was cut from the same filter paper.
Not controlled: width is the independent variable, the factor deliberately changed.
Controlled: every strip was measured after 10 minutes.
Not controlled: height is the dependent variable, the measured result.
Not controlled: the mean height is calculated from the dependent variable after the run.

why.correct: The means (6.1, 6.2, 6.0, 6.1 cm) differ by less than the spread within each width (strips of the same width differ by up to 0.5 cm). There is no trend with width.
options: Correct: the differences between means are smaller than the differences among repeats of the same width.
The means do not rise with width: 4.0 cm strips averaged the same as 0.5 cm strips.
The 0.5 cm mean (6.1 cm) is not the largest, and a 0.1 cm difference is far smaller than the variation among repeats.
A result showing no effect is a real finding when the design is sound; experiments test, they do not have to show a change.

why.correct: A testable question names one factor to change (paper type) and one result to measure (height in 10 minutes). Different papers have different fibers and spaces between them, so adhesion could differ.
options: Correct: one factor to change, one measurable result.
It asks about water "liking" something, a purpose, and names no measurable result.
"Most interesting" is an opinion; no measurement can answer it.
Paper does not want anything; the question cannot be tested by measurement.

why.correct: Moving air carries water vapor away from the surface and speeds evaporation. Because the fan was only in the 40 °C cabinet, the 40 °C group differed in two ways, so the extra loss cannot be credited to temperature alone. Air movement should have been a controlled variable.
options: Correct: two factors changed together, so their effects cannot be separated.
Three repeats is few, but the 40 °C dishes (6.9-7.5 g) do not overlap the others; the bigger problem is the second difference.
Every dish was weighed the same way, so weighing is the same in every group and cannot explain a difference.
The dependent variable is measured, not controlled, but that is how every experiment works, not a weakness.

why.correct: Mean loss at 30 °C = 4.0 g. Percentage = 4.0 ÷ 50.0 × 100 = 8%.

An if-then prediction starts with the independent variable (temperature), states the expected change in the dependent variable (mass lost) and gives a reason (more molecules can break free of their hydrogen bonds).
options: Correct: IV in the "if", DV in the "then", reason after "because".
This reverses the variables, and evaporation removes heat from what is left behind rather than releasing it.
This describes a controlled variable, not a prediction about the dependent variable.
This runs backward, from result to cause, and the reason simply repeats the claim.

why.correct: A control group gets the baseline condition (no warming) while everything else matches the experimental groups: same dishes, same mass, same cabinet type and the same time.
options: Correct: baseline temperature, everything else identical, with repeats.
A 50 °C group is another experimental group, not a no-warming baseline.
A sealed dish changes a different factor (open versus closed) and is a single dish, so it is not the baseline for open dishes.
Changing the mass of water adds a second difference instead of providing a baseline.

why.correct: The melting time is the result measured in response to the water temperature the student set.
options: Correct: it is measured, and it responds to the temperature.
The water temperature is set by the student: the independent variable.
The cube mass is kept equal: a controlled variable.
The volume should be kept the same: a controlled variable.

why.correct: Glass and plastic conduct heat differently. With two factors changed, any difference cannot be traced to salt. The container must be a controlled variable.
options: Correct: only the salt should differ.
Time to cool is a perfectly good dependent variable.
Comparing them is the point: salt is the independent variable.
A hypothesis helps planning, but data from a sound design are usable either way; the real flaw is the second variable.

why.correct: It names one factor to change (soap) and one result to measure (drops held).
options: Correct: one factor changed, one result measured.
"Most important" is a value judgment, not a measurement.
Molecules do not prefer anything, and the question names no factor to change.
"Should" asks for advice; it is not answered by a measurement.

why.correct: Single measurements vary. With repeats, you can see the spread within a group and judge whether the difference between groups is bigger than that spread.
options: Correct: repeats reveal chance variation.
Repeats do not change how accurate any one measurement is; they show how much measurements differ.
Matching results support a hypothesis but do not prove it.
Picking the best-fitting result is cherry-picking; every repeat is reported.

why.correct: One is a group for comparison; the other is a factor held constant across all groups.
options: Correct.
The factor the investigator changes is the independent variable, not a controlled variable.
They are different: one is a group, the other is a factor.
This swaps the two definitions.

why.correct: Question first, then what you change, what you measure, what you hold constant, and finally repeated runs.
Data can fail to support a prediction without proving the whole idea wrong. She measured final height at 10 minutes, while the prediction is about speed; the two can differ.
options: Correct: not supported for what was measured, and the mismatch between "faster" and "height at 10 min" is worth noticing.
One result does not prove an idea false for every case, and her measurement did not match the prediction's variable.
Both climbing is expected either way; support needs the predicted difference.
Warm versus cold already gives a comparison; a strip with no water would tell her nothing.

why.correct: A negative control should give no response. Water is treated exactly like the foods. Because it leaves no spot after 30 minutes, any lasting spot from a food cannot be blamed on wetness, the paper or the handling.
options: Correct: expected negative, treated identically, rules out a false positive from the method.
Oil is the positive control; it rules out a false negative.
The apple is a test sample, not a control, and its result says nothing about other plant foods.
Water is the right sample, but it rules out a spot made by the method, not water in the foods.

why.correct: The positive control checks that the test can give a "yes". If a known fat gives "no", the test is not working today (wrong paper, too little sample, wiped off), so other "no" results cannot be trusted.
options: Correct: a failed positive control makes negatives untrustworthy.
Matching a failed positive control shows the test is broken, not that the apple lacks fat.
Two blank results give no basis for ranking fat content.
A working negative control rules out false positives; it does nothing to rule out false negatives.

why.correct: Water also makes paper translucent until it evaporates. Wetness is a factor that differs between juicy and dry foods, so reading early lets it produce a false positive. The 30-minute wait, checked by the water control, removes it.
options: Correct: a temporary water spot, a false positive.
Fats do not evaporate at room temperature; that is why their spot lasts.
Water is polar and evaporates; lipids are the hydrophobic ones that stay.
Reading early adds false positives from water; the water control shows spots must last 30 minutes to count.

why.correct: With water blank and oil positive, a lasting faint spot points to a small amount of fat. The test is rough, so "less than the peanut" is as far as it goes.
options: Correct: a cautious claim matched to a cautious test.
A lasting spot, however faint, is a positive result once the water control shows the method makes none.
A faint spot suggests a little fat, not a sample that is all fat.
The oil positive control was run in the same session, so it covers the powder too.

why.correct: Distilled water is the negative control. It has no starch, so it should stay orange-brown. A blue-black result means starch got in from somewhere.
options: Correct: the negative control failed.
Starch solution is the positive control; blue-black is the expected result.
Potatoes store a lot of starch; blue-black is expected.
Oil is a lipid, not starch; it is not expected to turn blue-black.

why.correct: Every tube was rinsed in the same tub. Starch from the starch-solution tube or potato extract in that water would coat each tube, so even water and sugar test positive. The failed negative control reveals the contamination.
options: Correct: a shared source of starch explains positives in tubes that should be negative.
Table sugar is sucrose, a disaccharide (glucose + fructose), not a polysaccharide; it does not give the starch color.
If iodine alone turned blue-black, it would be useless as a starch test; the positive and negative colors differ.
Water does not turn into starch; dehydration synthesis joins monomers such as glucose and needs them to be present.

why.correct: A failed negative control means every result may be a false positive. The fix is to remove the cause (shared wash water) and rerun everything with both controls.
options: Correct: remove the cause, repeat with controls.
If the tubes were contaminated, the food results are untrustworthy too.
Hiding a failed control hides the problem; the control is what reveals it.
Tube 4 is explained by contamination, so it is not evidence that sugar contains starch.

why.correct: A sample known to contain starch should turn blue-black; it confirms the iodine is working.
options: Correct.
The negative control is distilled water, which lacks starch.
The independent variable is the type of sample, not one tube.
Starch solution is a known reference, not an unknown food.

why.correct: A confounding factor differs between groups and could affect the dependent variable. Different pans and stoves change how heat reaches each fat and how the temperature is read, so a difference could come from them rather than from the type of fat.
options: Correct: it differs between groups and plausibly affects the result.
Type of fat is the independent variable, the factor being tested.
Melting temperature is the dependent variable, the measured result.
Price differs, but price has no plausible effect on melting point; a confounding factor must also be able to change the result.

why.correct: A positive control is a sample known to contain what the test detects. Of these, only vegetable oil is a known fat.
options: Correct: a known fat.
Water has no lipid; it is a negative control.
Dye in water contains no lipid, so it shows nothing about whether the dye can color fat.
Sugar water is a carbohydrate solution with no fat; another negative.
An unknown cannot be a control, because its result is what you are trying to find out.

why.correct: Justifying a control means saying what it rules out: water lacks starch, so a negative result there shows the materials and method do not create a positive by themselves.
options: Correct: names what the control rules out.
Habit is not a reason, and water is not the right control for every test.
Easy visibility is convenient, but it says nothing about what the control rules out.
The control differs from the test tubes in exactly one respect (no sample), and this answer does not say what that shows.

why.correct: Water treated the same way checks that neither paper produces a lasting spot from the handling or from moisture.
options: Correct: same handling, no fat, both papers.
Oil is a known fat: a positive control.
Changing the reading time adds a second difference; it is not a control.
An untouched sheet skips the rubbing and wetting, so it would not reveal a spot made by the procedure.

why.correct: A positive control is known to give the response, so it shows the test can detect it under the conditions used.
options: Correct: it rules out false negatives.
That is the job of a negative control (false positives).
Changing the independent variable is the point of the experiment.
Repeats deal with chance variation, not a control.

why.correct: Both mass of sample and reading time differ between the groups and could change the grease spot, so a difference cannot be credited to brand alone.
options: Confounding: more chips make a bigger spot regardless of brand.
Confounding: reading later lets water spots fade, changing what counts.
Brand is the independent variable, the factor being compared.
Spot mass is the dependent variable, the measured result.
The paper is the same for both groups, so it is controlled.

why.correct: A failed negative control means something other than the sample is making the response. Oil carried on the students' fingers would put lipid on every spot, including the water control and the apple, which otherwise leaves no lasting spot.
options: Correct: contamination explains the failed negative control and the universal positives.
Fattier foods would not explain the water spot.
This predicts no spots at all, the opposite of what was seen.
Water is not a lipid; it evaporates from paper.

why.correct: A null hypothesis states that the independent variable (temperature) has no effect on the dependent variable (leakage): any differences are due to chance.
options: Correct: no effect.
This is an alternative hypothesis with a direction.
This is a prediction for two specific groups.
This is a proposed explanation of the effect, not a null hypothesis.

why.correct: The values overlap almost completely (0.05-0.11 and 0.06-0.12), and the 0.01 gap in means is far smaller than the 0.06 range within each group, so chance could easily produce it.
options: Correct: the difference is no bigger than chance variation.
Any two means differ a little; a difference must be larger than the variation within groups to count.
Data never prove "no effect"; a small effect could exist that four cubes cannot detect.
One high value is within the normal spread; it is not evidence of a real difference.

why.correct: The lowest 80 °C value (0.81) is about seven times the highest 20 °C value (0.11). A gap that large, with no overlap, is very unlikely to arise by chance.
options: Correct: reject the null; the data support the alternative.
Small samples can still show a clear difference when the gap is huge compared with the spread.
A slightly larger range does not cancel a difference this large.
Data support a hypothesis; they do not prove it for every case.

why.correct: Membranes are phospholipid bilayers held together by weak hydrophobic interactions, studded with proteins whose shape depends on weak bonds. High temperature loosens the bilayer and denatures the proteins, so the barrier fails and the water-soluble red substance escapes.
options: Correct: a disrupted barrier lets the substance out.
The substance is dissolved in water inside the cells; it does not evaporate in 1 minute of heating.
Squeezing would not explain a jump in leakage; the membranes are the barrier that fails.
One minute of heat does not make cells produce more substance; a damaged cell is not making anything.

why.correct: A directional alternative names which way the effect goes (higher temperature, more leakage).
options: Correct: it names a direction.
This is an alternative hypothesis without a direction.
This is the null hypothesis.
This changes the independent variable to cube size.

why.correct: The null says the independent variable (cholesterol) has no effect on the dependent variable (fluidity); the alternative says it does.
options: Correct.
Both statements claim an effect; neither is a "no effect" null.
This swaps the two.
Neither statement is about the independent variable, cholesterol.

why.correct: Without cholesterol the values run 1.9-2.3; with cholesterol 2.7-3.1. No overlap and a 0.8 µm²/s gap against ranges of 0.4 make chance an unlikely explanation.
options: Correct.
Data are judged on what they show. At low temperature cholesterol keeps phospholipids from packing tightly, which raises fluidity; there is no reason to dismiss the result.
A null hypothesis is never accepted, and here the groups clearly differ.
Six per group is enough when the groups do not overlap at all.

why.correct: At low temperature, phospholipid tails tend to pack closely and the membrane stiffens. Cholesterol's rigid rings sit between them and prevent tight packing, so the membrane stays more fluid. (At high temperature it has the opposite effect, restraining movement.)
options: Correct: it acts as a spacer in the cold.
Cholesterol does not break covalent bonds in other molecules.
Cholesterol does not chemically change the tails.
Cholesterol is a steroid (a lipid with four fused rings), not a protein.

why.correct: Only the independent variable (cholesterol) should differ. The phospholipids and the 10 °C temperature both affect fluidity, so they must be controlled.
options: Correct: both affect fluidity, so both are controlled.
Cholesterol is the independent variable; it is the one factor meant to differ.
Sideways speed is the dependent variable, the measured result.
Equal numbers of repeats are good practice, but the phrase "could differ freely" ignores that both groups had six; the factors that must match are those that affect fluidity.

why.correct: Failing to reject means the difference was not large enough to rule out chance. A small effect, too few repeats or high variability could hide a real effect, so the null is not "proved".
options: Correct: "not shown" is not the same as "shown not to exist".
Data never prove a null hypothesis.
A sound experiment that finds no effect has produced a real result.
Failing to reject the null gives no support to the alternative.

why.correct: The null says there is no relationship between the independent variable (salt concentration) and the dependent variable (spreading).
options: Correct.
This predicts an effect in one direction: an alternative.
An if-then prediction of an effect is not a null.
This states that a difference exists: an alternative.

why.correct: Decisions are made about the null: reject it or fail to reject it. Data support or fail to support an alternative; they never prove it, and a null is never accepted.
options: Correct.
"Prove" and "accept" overstate what data can do.
Nulls are not accepted; "fail to reject" is the correct phrase, and no effect is not shown.
More leakage at 80 °C is evidence against the null, and the decision is phrased backward.

why.correct: Null hypotheses state no difference or no relationship between the independent and dependent variables.
options: Null: no difference.
An alternative with a direction.
Null: no relationship.
An alternative: it predicts a difference.
A value judgment, not a testable hypothesis.

why.correct: The null makes a precise claim (no difference beyond chance). That lets you ask whether the data are too different from it to blame on chance. The alternative ("some effect") is too open to be checked directly.
options: Correct.
The null is often the opposite of what the investigator expects.
Nulls are never accepted, and the order of testing is not a rule.
The number of repeats depends on how variable the data are, not on which hypothesis is stated.

why.correct: Hypotheses come before data; data are analyzed; a decision is made about the null; the conclusion about the alternative follows.
Each group spans 1.2 µm²/s and most values overlap. A 0.4 gap in means is small against that spread, so the data do not show a real difference. More repeats might.
options: Correct.
A higher mean alone is not enough; it must be large compared with the variation.
One extreme value does not decide a comparison between groups.
Nulls are never accepted, and equal sample sizes say nothing about the result.

why.correct: A claim answers the question in one sentence that the data can support: the highest rate is at pH 7, with lower rates on both sides.
options: Correct.
The acidic rates (0.4 and 2.1) are among the lowest.
Lower activity is not destruction; the rates at pH 5 and 9 are still well above zero.
Activity rises to pH 7 and then falls; it does not rise steadily.

why.correct: Evidence quotes specific data with units and makes the comparison the claim depends on, including whether the difference is likely real.
options: Correct: numbers, units, comparison, uncertainty.
This is reasoning (a biological principle), not evidence from the data.
This is too vague: it names no values and does not show that pH 7 is highest.
Describing the method is not evidence, and repeats do not make a claim certain.

why.correct: Reasoning explains why the evidence supports the claim with a biological mechanism: pH alters ionic and hydrogen bonds involving R groups, changing the active site's shape and substrate binding.
options: Correct: a mechanism connecting pH to activity.
This restates evidence; it does not explain it.
True, but it does not explain why pH 7 gives the highest rate.
This is a purpose ("prefers", "needs"), not a mechanism.

why.correct: With gaps of 2 pH units, the data show the peak is near 7 but cannot locate it more precisely. Testing pH 6, 6.5, 7.5 and 8 would narrow it.
options: Correct: the spacing of the independent variable limits the claim.
Natural materials are fine; what matters is controlling variables.
Error bars show normal variation, not mistakes.
Oxygen is the easier product to measure, and it is released in proportion to the reaction.

why.correct: With X, rates are lower at low substrate but approach the same maximum as substrate rises (8.7 vs 9.5 µmol/min at 40 mM and still climbing). That pattern fits an inhibitor that competes for the active site.
options: Correct.
A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate however much substrate is added.
A denatured enzyme would not reach nearly the normal rate at high substrate.
X lowers the rate at every concentration tested.

why.correct: Competition predicts that extra substrate outcompetes the inhibitor, so the inhibitor's effect should shrink as substrate rises. The percentages show exactly that.
options: Correct: a shrinking effect with more substrate.
A single point does not show how the effect changes, which is the key to the claim.
This describes both curves; it does not distinguish the inhibitor's type.
Lower rates show inhibition, but any inhibitor does that; it does not show competition.

why.correct: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds the active site. Binding is reversible, so the more substrate there is, the more often substrate rather than X occupies the site.
options: Correct: competition for the active site explains the shrinking effect.
This describes noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibition, which would lower the maximum rate.
Substrate does not supply energy to the reaction; inhibitors interfere with binding or shape.
If X were converted to product, the total rate would not fall.

why.correct: The two types differ in what happens at very high substrate: a competitive inhibitor's curve reaches the same maximum; a noncompetitive one stays lower. At 40 mM the X curve is still rising, so higher concentrations would settle it.
options: Correct: it tests the distinguishing prediction.
Slowing the reaction does not separate the two kinds of inhibition.
This could be interesting but does not test the competitive versus noncompetitive pattern.
A different enzyme answers a different question.

why.correct: Sentence 3 is reasoning: it explains the evidence with a mechanism (denaturation changes the active site). Sentence 1 is the claim, 2 the evidence and 4 a limitation.
options: The claim: it answers the question.
The evidence: specific data with units.
Reasoning: a biological mechanism linking evidence to claim.
A limitation or source of error, not reasoning.

why.correct: The sentence is circular: it says the rate was highest because the rate was highest. Reasoning would explain, for example, how molecular motion and denaturation change the rate on either side of 37 °C.
options: Correct.
Numbers can appear in reasoning; the problem is the lack of a mechanism.
A single word does not explain anything.
Reasoning can and usually must refer to the variable; it explains its effect.

why.correct: Rising temperature increases molecular collisions (more enzyme-substrate complexes per second). Past the optimum, the extra motion disrupts hydrogen bonds and other interactions in the enzyme, changing the active site.
options: Correct: collisions up, then denaturation.
Enzymes do not copy themselves.
Activation energy is a barrier, not something heat adds; and there is no such limit on the active site.
Most substrates do not evaporate at 45 °C; the drop comes from the enzyme.

why.correct: A source of error is a problem with how measurements were made: inconsistent timing adds random variation. The others limit how far the conclusion extends.
options: Correct: a measurement problem.
A limit on how widely the result applies, not an error in measuring.
A limit set by the design (spacing of the independent variable).
A choice of scope; holding temperature constant was correct practice.

why.correct: Evidence comes from the data: numbers, units and a comparison (higher than, lower than, overlapping or not).
options: Correct.
Repeating the claim is not evidence.
A principle with no data is reasoning, not evidence.
The procedure is not evidence; the results are.

why.correct: Claim, evidence, reasoning; a strong answer then acknowledges a limitation.
The intervals (4.5-5.7 and 4.7-6.1) overlap, so the data cannot distinguish the two rates. A claim should not go further than the evidence.
options: Correct: the claim matches the evidence.
Overlapping intervals mean the difference is not shown.
Two temperatures cannot locate an optimum.
Two close temperatures say nothing about the effect of temperature over a wider range.

why.correct: Trace the block: no electron transfer to O₂, no pumping, the gradient falls, ATP synthase slows; NADH builds up, so fermentation rises to regenerate NAD⁺. Structures such as mitochondria do not change in minutes.

variables.name: O₂ used by the cells per minute
variables.why: Electrons can no longer be passed to O₂, so O₂ stops being reduced to water.

variables.name: H⁺ gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
variables.why: With electrons stuck, the chain stops pumping H⁺, while H⁺ keeps flowing back through ATP synthase, so the gradient runs down.

variables.name: ATP made by ATP synthase
variables.why: ATP synthase is driven by H⁺ flowing down its gradient; a shrinking gradient drives less synthesis.

variables.name: Lactate released by the cells
variables.why: NADH cannot unload electrons to the chain, so NAD⁺ runs short; fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ by reducing pyruvate to lactate, letting glycolysis continue.

variables.name: Number of mitochondria per cell
variables.why: Cyanide blocks a protein's function; in a few minutes it does not change how many mitochondria the cell has.

why.correct: The Krebs cycle needs NAD⁺ (and FAD) to accept electrons. With the chain blocked, NADH cannot be oxidized back to NAD⁺, so the cycle stalls even though it uses no O₂ itself.
options: Correct: a mechanism that links the block to the cycle through NAD⁺.
Need does not drive a pathway; without NAD⁺ the cycle cannot run faster.
It does not use O₂ directly, but it depends on NAD⁺ that only the chain regenerates in mitochondria.
The description says cyanide binds the last protein of the chain; the cycle slows indirectly.

why.correct: Cyanide does not keep O₂ out; it blocks its use. A full prediction names a measurable change (ATP falls, lactate rises) and the chain of causes from the block.
options: Correct: wrong mechanism, and no causal steps.
Exam predictions earn more credit with a mechanism, not less.
Fermentation yields far less ATP; cyanide does affect these cells.
A prediction with mechanism is expected to use "because".

why.correct: Isolated mitochondria have no glycolysis. If cyanide stops their O₂ use when given pyruvate, the effect is inside the mitochondrion, at the chain.
options: Correct: it isolates the system being tested.
A higher dose shows a bigger effect, not where it acts.
Glucose uptake reflects many steps; it does not separate glycolysis from the chain.
Without cyanide there is no test of cyanide's site of action.

why.correct: The block stops the flow of electrons from water through to NADP⁺, so O₂ release, NADPH and (through lost ATP and NADPH) carbon fixation all fall. The light supply is unchanged.

variables.name: O₂ released by water splitting
variables.why: Electrons cannot leave photosystem II, so it cannot accept new electrons from water, and water splitting stops.

variables.name: NADPH produced
variables.why: No electrons reach photosystem I and NADP⁺, so NADPH production stops.

variables.name: CO₂ fixed by the Calvin cycle
variables.why: The Calvin cycle needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions; with less of both, it slows.

variables.name: Light reaching the chloroplasts
variables.why: DCMU blocks electron flow; it does not change the lamp or how much light reaches the leaf.

why.correct: Photosystem II gives up electrons to the chain and refills them by splitting water, which releases O₂. If its electrons cannot move on, water splitting stops and O₂ release flattens.
options: Correct.
The description says DCMU binds a protein of the chain, not chlorophyll.
The Calvin cycle does not consume O₂, and DCMU acts on the chain.
The curve shows O₂ release stopping; nothing in the setup involves stomata.

why.correct: (2.7 − 0.9) µmol ÷ (15 − 5) min = 1.8 ÷ 10 = 0.18 µmol per disk per minute.
Trace the model: the compound gives electrons a new exit before the block, so photosystem II keeps working and water splitting, with O₂ release, resumes.
options: Correct: a model-based prediction.
The compound takes electrons before the block, so they no longer need to pass DCMU.
Nothing says the compound passes electrons to photosystem I; NADPH stays low.
The compound accepts electrons; it does not supply them, and O₂ comes from water.

why.correct: If DCMU acts only on light-driven electron flow, then in the dark treated and control disks should use O₂ (by respiration) at the same rate.
options: Correct: it tests the light dependence directly.
This tests whether more light overcomes the block, a different question.
More repeats improve precision but do not test light dependence.
Timing does not address whether light is required.

why.correct: An uncoupler separates electron flow from ATP synthesis: the chain runs (O₂ use up), but the gradient leaks away as heat rather than driving ATP synthase.

variables.name: ATP made by ATP synthase
variables.why: H⁺ returns through the leak instead of through ATP synthase, so less ATP is made.

variables.name: Heat released by the mitochondria
variables.why: Energy in the gradient is released as heat when H⁺ leaks back instead of doing work in ATP synthase.

variables.name: O₂ used by the electron transport chain
variables.why: With the gradient dissipated, nothing holds back pumping, so electrons flow faster to O₂.

variables.name: Number of electron transport proteins
variables.why: An uncoupler opens a leak; it does not change how many chain proteins the membrane holds.

why.correct: Competitive inhibitors bind the active site reversibly. At high substrate, substrate wins most of the binding events, so the rate approaches the uninhibited maximum.
options: Correct.
That describes a noncompetitive inhibitor.
High substrate does not block binding; it fills sites with substrate.
Inhibitors are not converted to substrate.

why.correct: Aquaporins let water cross membranes quickly. Blocked, they slow osmosis out of the tubule, so more water stays in the urine.
options: Correct.
Blocked channels slow water movement in both directions; they do not pull more in.
Water can cross slowly through the bilayer, but most rapid movement is through aquaporins.
Aquaporins are selective for water, not ions.

why.correct: Start at the perturbation, say what stops working, follow each effect to the next, end at something you can measure.
It names the change (ATP falls) and the cause in steps (H⁺ bypasses ATP synthase).
options: Correct.
A prediction with no mechanism.
A judgment with effects, but no mechanism linking them.
Too vague to test, and no mechanism.

why.correct: Isolated mitochondria given pyruvate bypass glycolysis. If O₂ use still falls, the drug acts inside the mitochondrion; if not, an earlier step is more likely.
options: Correct.
A dose response confirms an effect but not where it acts.
Temperature changes everything; it does not locate the drug's target.
Lower glucose uptake fits either explanation.
